utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Sarah Clanton; Case Manager, Indah Susanti; and legal interns, Katherine Davis; Max Dalton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, Negosava Smiljanic, and Milan Jovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we proceed with Mr. Hadzic's testimony, there is the little issue about lifting the private session designation in the transcript not from yesterday but from the day before. I understand that parties agree upon three of the suggestions Mr. Stringer made. And for the fourth, Mr. Zivanovic, do you have a position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have the position. Our position is that this part of transcript should be keep in -- in the -- in the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We will check that. And, in the meantime, if parties could provide the Registrar with the exact reference in the French transcript, please. Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, in 1992, was Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, part of your core of body-guards or your security detail?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please P1845. It is tab 1282.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are conclusions of the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see the session was held on 16 April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I see that it is strictly confidential. I don't know whether it should be -- it -- maybe it should not be broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's a public exhibit, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, it could be broadcasted, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Hadzic, this session discussed various matters, but I should like you to focus on a passage where you are mentioned in the same context as Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In e-court, it's page 65 in the original and 68 in English. In fact, it's page 63 of the record itself. In e-court, it's 65. Can we turn back two pages just to see who is speaking here. That means page 63 of the original and page 66 of the translation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the words of General Zivota Panic at this session of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now we can go back to pages 65 and 68 in Serbian and in English respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He says, among other things: "Arkan is managed about Hadzic, or led by Hadzic. I was in Knin yesterday and they were all wondering, in one way or another, what Arkan was doing in the area. He is taking him around as some sort of body-guard. Somebody should call President Hadzic to tell him to remove Arkan from this area." Considering that he is referred to here as a member of your corps of body-guards, I'd like to know did anyone call you in 1992 to ask you to remove from your area Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And this is the first time I see this. I mean, I saw it for the first time after I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It follows from this that, at that time, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was in Knin, and it was a problem that he was there. I'd like to know where you were generally in that period. I'm not asking about a specific date. Where did you spend most of your time in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, for the most part, in Eastern Slavonia, where I was born, or in Serbia, where my family was. And in April, I even travelled to Russia to take my son to a doctor. I didn't go frequently to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that he's referred to here as a member of your body-guard detail, did he follow you? Did he accompany you when you went to -- from Knin to Novi Sad, or -- did he travel around with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was never a member of my body-guard detail. And he didn't travel around with me. He always went where he pleased. I was never informed what he was doing or where he was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Generally, at this time, when you were either president of the government of -- or, rather, prime minister of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or the president of RSK, did you have any capacity to issue him orders, to arrest him, to remove him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't. Moreover, I had the feeling that it could be the contrary, the other way around, as far as arrest is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, "the other way around"? Could you be more precise.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have him arrested because I did not have much personnel. His personnel was ten times larger than mine. He was stronger than I. That's why I thought he could arrest me, rather than I him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move to page 67 of the original and the page 70 in English. Maybe we should go one extra -- before that it is page 66 and -- in B/C/S and 69 in English just to see who spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now Borisav Jovic took the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we can go back to page 67 in B/C/S and 70 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He says -- no, that's not a starting point --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. It is -- Borisav Jovic is on the next page of English translation. No, no. No. That's correct page, sorry. It was correct page. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "As far as these Eagles and Arkan are concerned, I think the army should arrest them pursuant to our instructions." To the best of your knowledge, was the army able to do that on the instructions of the Presidency of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency was the Supreme Command of the Yugoslav People's Army, and if they had issued such an order, I believe they would have been able to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then Zivota Panic speaks and says: "No. The MUP, it's Ministry of Interior, should do that." And then Borisav Jovic speaks again and says: "No. That's not a starting point for us." And then he explains why. In your estimate, was the Ministry of the Interior able to achieve that? I suppose they meant the MUP of Yugoslavia or Serbia.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the MUP could have done it, as well as the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then Borisav Jovic speaks again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's at the bottom of the page, the last paragraph in English. He says: "So if the army can take up this task, I would gladly give them this task, and if they catch them in the act, they should dismiss them and arrest them." Correction, "... they should disarm and arrest them." Then let's move to the next page in the original and in English. Zivota Panic replies: "There is no task that the army cannot execute, as long as the Supreme Command orders it. If the Supreme Command orders us to move out of Bosnia tomorrow, we will do it very simply, et cetera." Tell me, in April 1992, when this session of the Presidency took place, were the authorities of the SFRY capable of carrying out such an operation outside of Serbia, let's say, in the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because, officially, it was still a single state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then Zivota Panic speaks again and he says: "I consider it an order: We will arrest all paramilitary organisations appearing in this area." According to your knowledge, was this order implemented?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, and I never heard that. No one spoke about this. This information never reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that, Jugoslav Kostic says: "Zivota, at a session here once I asked what was the relationship between Arkan and the JNA and you personally told me that it was good." Can you tell us who was Jugoslav Kostic at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jugoslav Kostic was a member of the Presidency of the SFRY on behalf of the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina, so he was on equal footing with Borisav Jovic and everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move to the next page of translation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the further text, Zivota Panic says the following: "Arkan carried out tasks very well in this area. At one point he broke away but they brought him back, et cetera. However, he is doing Yugoslavia a disservice." And can we move to the following page of the original, please: "He should be called and given a task. Those who sent him there should call him. I don't know who sent him. However, Arkan happened to be in Bijeljina, in Zvornik, around Sarajevo, and Knin, and so on. Someone is leading him and giving him tasks. We should see who is doing this. It is certain that we are not giving him any tasks. However, there is a difference between Arkan and Jovic. Jovic's men should be arrested immediately. They are mostly the worst kind. They were sort of criminals." Can you tell us which Jovic is referred to here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that it's Mirko Jovic from Pazova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Panic then continued by saying: "Arkan is very disciplined when he performs tasks. However, his patrons should be the ones to call him. I will complete my task honourably because this is in the interests of Serbia and the new Yugoslavia." From what you know, did Arkan carry out the tasks he was given by the army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did, even though I have no direct knowledge. I did not take part in their agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I have the technical problems. My screen is black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for a technician to come, Mr. Zivanovic. Perhaps it's a good idea to close your microphone in the meantime. Is it okay now, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No? Okay. We had the same problem, but here it's solved. Back in business, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by what you could observe about the relations between Arkan and the officers, especially the high-ranking officers of the former JNA, could you tell us if this accurately reflects the situation; namely, that he was disciplined when executing tasks and that he was on good terms with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understood that he was a part of the JNA and that he did carry out tasks he got from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P2715.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Tab number 742. However, it is -- we put on our list as 1D328. And, meanwhile, we established that it was already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, I think that you have already had an opportunity to see this document. It is an interview of General Panic given to the media in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move to page 32, English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll return to this document later because the page numbers that I have are not correct. [In English] May we see, please, P2649. It is tab 599.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, can you see that this is a document issued from the General Staff of the SFRY armed forces on the 12th of March, 1992. It has to do with the work of the staffs and units of the TO units in the course of mobilisation and demobilisation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you were the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina at the time and, as we saw yesterday, you had certain duties with regard to the army or, rather, the Territorial Defence at the time. I'd like to know whether you received this document.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, nor was I familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move to P2650, please. It's tab 1298.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the Federal Secretariat of National Defence and it deals with the establishing of the forming of rear bases of TO in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Now, as you were discharging the duty as the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina at the time, I wanted to ask you whether you knew about the forming of these TO rear bases in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Were you informed about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about it, nor was I informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The names of five military personnel are listed here, of which two, I think, are from the Federal Secretariat of National Defence -- or, rather, three of them, or even four. Could you tell me whether you knew anyone of them? Did you have a chance to see them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know them. I never saw them. And this is the first time I hear these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could you tell us whether, during 1991 or 1992 while you were the prime minister of the Serbian area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, was there a security service within your government or one of its ministries?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. While the government of SAO SBWS had its term in office, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1834. It is tab 418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the document number Mr. Zivanovic, please. It's not on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It is P1834, tab 418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report dated 5th March 1992 and relates to January and February that year. First of all, are you familiar with this document? Were you aware of it while you were prime minister of the Serbian district; and, if so, when did you see it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of it. I saw it for the first time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you infer from this report, although it's not written in so many words, to whom it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He's asking the witness to simply speculate here. I think if the witness doesn't know anything about the report, it's just asking for speculation. It's not helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not speculation because it is -- he could conclude from the text of this document if he knows the organ or where this document was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It would still be guessing, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that in the beginning of that year - that is to say, 1992 we don't have a date - the Ministry of Interior of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem established a State Security Service based in Vukovar with a temporary base in Dalj. Tell me, who controlled the Ministry of Interior of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally the minister was Predrag Radlovic at the suggestion of Badza, but it was actually controlled by Badza and his men who had, by that time, arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of the Interior or anyone else inform the government that the State Security Service had been established?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, we read that this department operated for a short time within the SUP of Vukovar but then it was decided after joint consultations that the service was not fully operative in that form and the Ministry of the Interior decided that the State Security Service should continue to work independently with the proviso that co-operation with the SJB - that is to say, the public security service - be promoted to the maximum. It says here that after joint consultation, a joint estimate was made. Whose joint estimate was it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who made that estimate jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say afterwards, taking upon themselves full responsibility for possible consequences that could ensue from such work and operation, the employees of the department, with the approval of the MUP, organised themselves and used the working potential and experience to formulate thrusts of their work. Was there any such self-organisation, to the best of your knowledge, of the employees of that department?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. And from my very modest knowledge about these things, it sounds illogical to me. I would have understood it if they had organised themselves in the area of public security to preserve law and order, prevent robberies, et cetera. But I don't know how the state security can organise themselves, the interests of which state would they be protecting and what positions would they have defended, I really can't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the next page of this document, reference is made to thrusts of activity or operation. And, among other things, it says that they had established a series of contacts with Town Commands, with Territorial Defence Staffs, with the public security service, the court, the prosecutor's office, and the security service of the JNA. Were you aware of the contacts that this service had? Did any of the persons in Town Commands, the TO, or the other services mentioned here, ever tell that you that they had contacts with this service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me. To be honest, I had no particular contact with all the people you enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, we read, among other things as follows: Based on the information jointly collected so far, a register of pursuits has been made, copied, and made available to all organisational units. Do you know about this register?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me what kind of organisational units are mentioned here? Because this department had eight employees, including only five operatives, as we see in paragraph 2 on page 1.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this. My inference is that they wanted to introduce themselves to somebody, but not to me and not the government. I think they may have tried to present their credentials to the MUP in Knin, to the MUP of the RSK in Knin. That document was written when the Republic of Serbian Krajina had already been established in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On -- at the end of page 3, straddling page 4, there is talk about a certain co-operation with the security service of the JNA. It says that this security service offered them some rolling stock, proper equipment. And, on the next page, it says that these organs had duly informed the Secretariat for National Defence. Did you know anything about this? Did the security service of the JNA or somebody from the JNA or the National Defence Secretariat inform you of any -- of this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this, and they were not required to keep me informed. It was still part of the SFRY territory, and they had agencies there still that were independent of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. It was all within the area covered by the JNA, and now I see it was also agreed with the security service of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the next page, page number 5, in the middle of the page, we read the following: "Namely, at this time of disrupted values and general mistrust and aware of the advantages they have and without trusting the public security service or the State Security Service, the State Security Service established security services like the Serbian National Security and the security services in the TO Staffs. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's, unit is also used for this purpose." Could you comment on this passage.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Serbian National Security, I've already explained. It didn't exist. It was just misinformation spread among the people. As for the security services of TO Staffs and that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was used for these purposes, I hear of this for the first time now. I don't think it's true, but I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further below, it says: "Here we primarily mean the illegal creation of positions within the public security service by the Serbian National Security which has been proven without a doubt." Do you know anything about this? Any of these people who guarded the government building, did they have any positions in the public security service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know these men until they started guarding the government. But from what I know, none of them were former policemen or had ever worked for the police force or had any connection to the police, but I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Below, we read that dissatisfaction culminated when it became known that the session of the Assembly of Krajina on the 25th of February, 1992, was guarded by the Serbian National Security and the unit of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. You were at that assembly session. Do you know who organised the security detail and who was on that security detail, if you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main security was organised by the Yugoslav People's Army, as there were guests from the federal state present. Whenever they came, since the time of Borovo Selo in 1991 and then in 1992, it was always the JNA that did it independently. As for those that he calls the Serbian National Security, there were a couple of them there, but they brought some ministers and they came as the escorts. So, in total, perhaps ten of them may have been there, and five may have stayed on in Erdut to watch over the empty building, so maybe there were three, or four or five. Arkan was doing it as part of the JNA but he wasn't present inside. As far as I remember, he didn't attend the session. It is possible that his men provided security in the street, together with the JNA. But I didn't know the protocol. The main part of it was defined in co-operation with the federal government which provided some resources and technical assistance. We were still a part of the federal state at the time. So administration documents, photocopying machines, that was all provided by the federal institutions which I only accidentally heard. I didn't think that somebody from the federal protocol had been there and assisted with organising it, but that was done independently from me, without consulting me at any point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat about this last issue you told us about. Who came to organise all this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some people from the federal protocol of the federal state in Belgrade helped Ilija Koncarevic to organise it all. I met a man. They introduced him to me. I knew his name, but I can't remember it at the moment. I remember now. His last name was Simendic [phoen]. I think it was Bogdan Simendic. There were some others whose names I didn't know, but they were, I think, employees of the federal Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could you tell us as there is a signature, or, rather, just a typed name at the end of the document of the chief of the SDB department, Slobodan Pezikovic [phoen], so it's not handwritten. But do you know who this person is; and, if so, can you give us some more details about him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who that is. I didn't know him personally at the time. He was employed by the Croatian State Security Service. I think that he was working in Osijek before the war. As I was on good terms with this service in Vinkovci, I had heard his name but I had never met him. I only met him later. The government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina later appointed him as the chief of the RDB of all of Krajina. But it may have been later, perhaps in 1993, though I don't remember exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, yesterday you talked about the action on the Miljevic plateau. I would now show you -- we won't play the video that was shown on TV, but we'll just look at the surrogate sheet. It's 1D467, tab 764. Do you remember the details described herein in this report, with regard to the way this action developed and when the action at the Miljevici plateau took place. In a word, does this correspond with the information you had about this action. Is it a true report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date corresponds. It was the 21st of June, 1992. Some details are left out, but everything that's unfavourable for the Croatian side, and whatever could be positive, they mention it. But, more or less, it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what are the details that have been left out and that you believe are also important for this action.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how important they are, but I received information that, on the previous day, before the action was launched, some women on the Croatian side brought wine and distributed it to the Serbian fighters so that they got drunk. But it was a mistake on part of these people to have accepted that and that they were sleeping at the moment when the action began. I heard it in an informal conversation with some of those who survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if there were any casualties, civilians, in particular, during this Croatian offensive?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that there were casualties, both civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the civilian population which was present in the area where the Croatian forces carried out these combat operations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, all of those civilians were expelled from this territory. Likewise, unfortunately again, no one else seemed to be interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you imply by nobody else? Who do you imply by that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally the international community. I wouldn't name anyone in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As, in a way, Yugoslavia guaranteed the Vance Plan to you, did you or the organs of the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina complain to the Yugoslav authorities so that they would take any steps to prevent such attacks?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any specific steps. We did everything that we could. At the time, the so-called Zabljak constitution had already been adopted and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had been established and one could already see that we were completely abandoned in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tendered this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us about operations conducted in 1993 around the Medak pocket. I would like to show you some documents relating to these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D737. It is tab 781.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the indictment issued by this Tribunal against the Croatian General Janko Bobetko. I would like us to look at paragraph 28. It's on page 5. It reads that during the Medak pocket operation, at least 100 Serbs, including 29 local Serb civilians, were unlawfully killed while others sustained serious injuries. Many of the civilians who were killed and wounded were women and elderly people. The murder of five Serbian soldiers who had been taken prisoner, or hors de combat, are also mentioned. Their names are included in the schedule to the indictment, and it's not necessary for us to see that right now. My question is whether these allegations correspond to the information you had about the operation in the Medak pocket.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could please look at paragraph 29 as well, which reads that: Approximately 164 homes and 146 [as interpreted] barns and outbuildings were destroyed in the villages within the Medak pocket, mostly by fire and explosives, after the Croatian forces had already taken control of the area. Does that correspond with some of the information you had about the events which took place at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond. I remember that General Novakovic told me because I was a layman when it came to military issues, so I remember that. He said that they had such artillery preparation that they would hit practically every metre and that was a signal for us that the Croats were well armed. They practically plowed all this area with their artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 30 reads that in the same period property of the Serb civilians was plundered by the Croatian forces, or by persons in civilian clothes supervised by the Croatian forces and that these included personal belongings, household goods, building materials, furniture, farm animals, that is to say, livestock, agricultural machinery and other equipment. Does that correspond with the information you had?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We object to that, Mr. President. If indictments were admissible to prove the allegations contained inside them, then why have a trial? Mr. Hadzic was the president of the RSK at the time of the events described. He's -- says that he knows about these things happening. It's his belief that these things happened. The Chamber has that evidence in the form of his testimony. And so the indictment in a case in which -- never resulted in a trial or a judgement really doesn't have any probative value. We object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The indictment is a legal act and it would be adduced into evidence too, and it doesn't prove the guilt of the accused but just some facts alleged in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection -- the objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could you look at 1D732, tab 594. It's a report from a meeting in Geneva on the 16th of June, 1993 -- no, it's 14 June, 1993. Or 16. I'm slightly confused by these dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I'm a little bit confused with the tab number. You said 594; right? And then the document number would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the tab number would be 1D732 on -- the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It is -- it must be my error. Sorry. Tab 779.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 779. That would be better, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This relates to a meeting scheduled to take place in Geneva on 16 June and it provides a certain appraisal. I'd like to quote to you one passage from paragraph 2. It says: [In English] "One hears a great deal in Knin, at present, of not a square inch of Krajina, et cetera, and of the rejection by one of their assemblies at Okucani of the 802 draft agreement on 6 April. All those associated with the 6 April agreement are held in suspicion by the RSK military, including President Hadzic, and any mention of Misa Milosevic provokes nasty and dismissive remarks." [Interpretation] I'd like to ask you: Do you remember that agreement of 6th April that gave rise to such suspicions and your name is specifically mentioned in the context of these suspicions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that those talks followed the Croatian operation Maslenica and they were supposed to diffuse tensions. I was faced with that kind of problem from the very beginning, from my arrest at Plitvice almost to this day, that somebody is working for the other side, et cetera. Such comments could often be heard from extremists and that happened again when I advocated the release of the Maslenica bridge which would connect the north of Croatia with the south of Croatia. First of all, it was Babic's followers who attacked me, and there were some people who thought the same within the army. Yes, I -- I know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us how these suspicions about you, spread by Babic and his followers, developed later? Did they diminish, or did they grow?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not only Babic's followers. There were also some services in Serbia who spread this, and it escalated with time, sometimes resulting in open clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. We'll take the first break. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: A short oral ruling. On the 1st of July, the Defence filed a motion to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The Defence indicated that it intended to uses 47 documents included in the motion with Mr. Hadzic during his testimony and requested that they be dealt with on an expedited basis. On 3 July, the Chamber gave an oral ruling in which it allowed 14 of the 47 documents to be added to the exhibit list. Included in the remaining 32 documents are -- sorry, included in the remaining 33 documents are 32 documents which were provided to the Defence by Serbia on the 3rd of January, 2014. At the time of the motion, 25 of these documents had not been translated into English. The Chamber noted that it would consider the addition of these documents after all the translations had been provided and it had received a full response from the Prosecution. With the exception of one document, Rule 65 ter number 1D01935, the English translation for each of the 32 documents has now been uploaded and released in e-court. The Prosecution filed a written response to the motion on 15 July, 2014. After considering -- I'm sorry. After considering the submissions of the parties, the Chamber is satisfied that, taking into account the specific circumstances of this case, good cause has been shown for amending the Defence's exhibit list to include the 31 documents provided by Serbia for which an English translation has been provided. While the Chamber considers that the Defence has not demonstrated due diligence in adding the documents to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list, the documents are relevant and of sufficient importance to justify addition at this stage of the trial. The Chamber is satisfied that the addition of the documents will not result in undue prejudice to the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber remains seized of the motion in all other respects. Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, we still have on the screen the document we discussed before the break, and I wanted to ask you this: Since you said this distrust towards you escalated, could you tell us in what way? What happened? What was done against you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, all this lasted a long time, and fear was spread among the people that I might betray the interests of the people of Krajina, that I was close to the Croatian side, and they even went so far to call me a Croatian spy, which, of course, was untrue. And that caused me great problems, distracting me from dedicating myself to my work and the negotiations. And whatever my opponents did not like in my work, they would say, That's what Hadzic agreed with Croatia but it's in Croatian interests, not ours. And the same happened at the signing of the Erdut Agreement, although it was accepted by Babic and by the deputies of the Serbian Radical Party. Their main argument was that I betrayed the interests of Krajina and violated the constitution because I had agreed to an agreement whereby, in a village in Dalmatia, which the Croatians, by the way, had occupied in the Maslenica operation and which should have been returned to us, I had agreed that only five Serb policemen remain there. That was a minor point, but they interpreted it by saying, It's against the constitution. We should have been able to put there as many policemen as we want to, which was nonsense because no more than five policemen were needed there, in the first place. But, anyway, it gave them a reason to attack me and to have the agreement dismissed by the assembly; whereas, I spent all my time explaining that this agreement was good for us, that it brings peace, and renewed peaceful co-existence with other people. But it was all in vein.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned the Erdut Agreement. Can you tell us what kind of agreement it was, when was it concluded, and what were its main provisions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, it was in the middle of July 1993. I think it was the 16th of July, but I'm not quite sure. Our delegation negotiated separately with international negotiators and mediators who then negotiated with the Croatian side and shuttled between us. So we came to an agreement with a lot of mediation, agreeing ultimately on almost all issues. Croatia was supposed to finally implement the resolution of the Security Council, I think the number was 802, and return to their positions before the Maslenica operation. In other words, to go back from the Perusa dam and all the other points it had occupied in operation Maslenica. That agreement was signed unconditionally by the Croatian side, and President Tudjman authorised his delegation to sign it. And on the Serbian side, it was signed by our foreign minister, Slobodan Jarcevic. And our signature was conditional because it had to be ratified by the assembly, since both Jarcevic and I were elected by the assembly. I managed to conduct consultations with deputies to the assembly from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem who realised that this agreement would bring about peace and they were in favour of the agreement; whereas, deputies from the Knin area listened to Babic and rejected the agreement, and that led to the development that culminated in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the document that is still on the screen, a name is mentioned, Misa Milosevic, at the very beginning. Could you tell us who was this person and what connections did he have, both with you and with the Republic of Serbian Krajina in general, or SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Misa Milosevic was and maybe still is - I don't know as I'm not in touch with him anymore - the general secretary of the International Serbian Organisation, which has a seat in Geneva. He used to know Mr. Babic and the members of their delegation, and I met him at some of the negotiations that we went to in the month of October. Mr. Babic engaged him to represent the interests of the SAO Krajina before our meetings when I still did not know him, and they had known each other from before. In later negotiations, both in Geneva and in New York, Mr. Milosevic was a kind of a technical person for us who was in charge of the protocol and assisted us, and he did a lot for us in that sense, but he did not influence the policy of the government or the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please just repeat his function and the organisation that he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the secretary-general of the World Serbian Community seated in Geneva. It was an organisation that represented the Serbs from the diaspora. This position of secretary-general was a permanent one, and the president was elected for a specific term, a year or two. It was a well known person from Serbia. At the time when I co-operated with Mr. Milosevic, the president of this organisation was the Academician, Antonije Isakovic, the late Antonije Isakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now go back to 1D328, tab 742. It's been admitted as P2715. It's an interview from 1994 which General Zivota Panic gave to the media. In it, he talked a lot about the war events from 1991, 1992, and 1993. We'll look at page 26 of the original, which corresponds to page 25 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could look at the last sentence at the bottom of the page in B/C/S. Yes. If you can look at that, please, where it reads: "They included Arkan's Tigers and Seselj's Chetniks. They were not big groups, say, in Arkan's case say between 80 and 120 persons and in Seselj's case between 90 and 120 men. All these formations" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please turn to the following page in the original:

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "However, all these formations were under my command, where I placed them. They performed the tasks of the unit to which they were attached. But the units who wanted to act independently were removed from that area. We disarmed them immediately and sent them away." Please tell me, according to the information you had - if you had any - whether this corresponds to the situation which existed in SBWS in 1991.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does reflect the situation. When I got here, I received documents and orders which confirmed that. There was a direct order issued by Panic to the effect that everyone who was not a member of the JNA should be expelled back to Serbia and disarmed, and whoever was not disarmed meant that they were part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please move to page 36 in B/C/S, which corresponds to page 34 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this segment of the text, the general -- the journalist asks a question about Arkan's Tigers. He asked General Panic what the co-operation with them was like. And General Panic says: "Arkan came to that area before the army was engaged. I suppose he had some arrangements with the local leaders in the area. I don't know what kind of arrangements, but he formed his only units which controlled and observed the area around Dalj to the north of Vukovar, just like that." Could you tell me whether according to the information you had this is correct or not. First of all, that Arkan had come to the area when the JNA was not yet there.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. It seems improbable to me that Zivota Panic didn't have true information. It seems to me that he wanted to avoid telling the truth on purpose here. From what I learned later, Arkan first came to Tenja. That was close to Osijek rather than Vukovar. And the JNA was already in Tenja at the time. Because after the 7th of July and the Croatian attack on Tenja, the JNA separated the warring parties and stayed on in Tenja. So the JNA had already been there then just as it had been in Borovo Selo from the 2nd of May onwards. In the Dalj area, Arkan appeared after the 1st of August, much later than the time when the JNA arrived there, and it arrived on the 1st of August. So what Panic said is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He further says: "Since we came here, we could see that he had his own units and did his own business," and so on, "I then called the commander from the area. I ordered that he be summoned, that he should place him under his command and he would then appoint them. If he didn't want to do it, he would have to leave the area. He accepted that immediately. When I did a tour of duty of units north of Vukovar towards Osijek, in some populated places, I could see his units, his troops. He lined them up immediately and he gave me a report. It was a brief report." Can you tell me whether this reflected the actual situation on the ground and, in particular, do you know whether General Panic ever came to SBWS or that part of it and did a tour of duty of the units which were deployed so that they were facing Osijek?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is true what the situation on the ground was like and that Arkan acted in co-ordinated action and was under full control of the Yugoslav People's Army. As for General Panic's visit, he didn't inform me about this, and I didn't know that. But he didn't inform me at the time. I didn't know that, nor did he consider that he ought to report to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I apologise for the interruption. Mr. President, I was going to ask whether it might be necessary to clarify what was said at page 29, line 19. I don't know whether the witness misspoke or whether there was an interpretation issue. He said: "In the Dalj area, Arkan appeared after the 1st of August, much later than the time when the JNA arrived there, and it arrived on the 1st of August." And I don't know if that is perhaps something to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you please clarify. When did the JNA arrive in Dalj and when did Arkan appear in Dalj, from what you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA arrived in Dalj on the 1st of August, 1991, which is general knowledge. And I perhaps made a mistake. I think mathematically, so I said quite some time after. I thought it was mathematically clear. I believe that it was certain that he did not arrive together with the army and especially not before them. Much later means ten or 15 days at least, perhaps more. In my view, it is much time because he didn't come on the 1st of August when the army did arrive. He may have come in late August and then he stayed on, because he showed up once in Dalj in mid-August. But it was only in mid-September that he settled there. So that's what I meant. It wasn't a matter of years but perhaps weeks or months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we also clarify another thing, please. You told us when you saw him first. Could you tell us who did he arrive with and when was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was around mid-August or in the first half of August. He came together with Badza. I have already said who was with them, and I later remembered when we discussed the certificates signed by Milanovic when he assigned the TO commander, that Zika Trajkovic was also with them then. I hadn't known him at the time. I learned later who he was. He also held a high position within the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In which police force did he occupy a high position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further below in the document, we see that General Panic saw immediately that the members of his unit were disciplined, well equipped, well trained, and that they "listen only to Arkan." And he says, "At that time, there were 83 of them. Later on, the number increased." Now, from what you were able to see there, did you have the same impression in terms of the discipline of that unit and their obedience to Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my conclusion, from my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will skip over one bit until the reference to the fact that he did go into populated areas but only after the army. It says: "The army would take it. Then he would go into that populated area and because the army is the army, the army goes through, finishes the business normally, whereas the units which come later, they do the business in populated areas. He sometimes played that role, the role of those other units who are supposed to go into populated areas. It's certain that they did carry out tasks, everything that the army gave them, until the moment when the army no longer needed them." Do you know how the unit of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, functioned in that role in those operations with the army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about these technical matters. I was never present when they agreed these things, but I understood that they were working together. I'm not saying this is not true, but it is not the same as my thinking. If we look at what Panic says, it turns out that Arkan was some sort of logistical unit holding already occupied territory. My understanding was that his units were going ahead, but I wasn't ever a witness, nor did anyone ever officially tell me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of that sentence, it says: "However, Goran Hadzic was the president of that Serbian Krajina. He kept him as his own body-guard." Is this true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying this for at least the third time before this Court: It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further below, the journalist says that somebody told him that Arkan was very arrogant in his treatment of lower-ranking officers, and he asks General Panic: "Did you ever receive a report about this? Did you hear these stories? And what was it really like?" And General Panic answers: "While I was in command and during the Vukovar operation, that did not happen. But I heard that in Knin, I believe in the Knin Krajina, now after all these things are over, that there were some differences and clashes." Could you please comment on this, especially in the light of those security reports that were sent precisely to the Command of the 1st Military District and specifically General Panic. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I had occasion to read those reports since I've come here, and it's obvious from them that Panic is not telling the truth. But I had first-hand information, as I said at the beginning of my testimony. Dragomir Lastavica, who was a reserve captain first class in charge of supplies in Erdut told me that Arkan slapped around this lieutenant-colonel in Erdut and kicked him in the butt. He was there at the time and he knew that. Now, I don't know what Zivota Panic heard and from whom, but this incident happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you cannot confirm that those reports from security organs ever reached him.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they did, but I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On this page, the journalist asks General Panic if he discussed these problems with Kadijevic, with Cosic. And Panic answers that when he became the chief, the Supreme Defence Council discussed it and he mentioned Milosevic, the then-president of Yugoslavia Cosic, Bulatovic, and Adzic saying that this problem was raised. Out of all these people who are listed - Kadijevic, Milosevic, Cosic, Bulatovic, Adzic - did any of them either tell you this directly or let you know about this through some other channels? Did they in any way give you the information about this problem that exists on the ground that is caused by Arkan and his units, and did they ever ask you to do something about it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard anybody discussing it, and I even didn't know about these complaints against Arkan and his actions. I was once confronted with a case that I didn't mention during proofing because I only now remember it. Arkan caused a problem in a village close to mine, Trpinja. He started trading in spirits. And in Trpinja, he barged into a house where people were making rakija. He overturned their caldron and beat them up. I heard about this because it is a neighbouring village, and I heard about it in the local cafe. And at a discussion in Belgrade in President Milosevic's office, we were discussing something related to the UNPROFOR. I told him about the problem we were facing there, but President Milosevic did not give me a sympathetic ear. He said he will inquire into it with some people, without naming them, and he said, Well, he has his own members of parliament, I don't know what to do about him, and I realised he wasn't going to do anything. But that's all about -- that's all I know about these activity, such as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just clarify this for the record: What was this about making rakija, the local brandy, that Arkan didn't like?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, almost every household in our parts makes plum brandy. Plums are left to ripen and then it's all distilled in this caldron. It's called the Slivovitz, the plum brandy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did these people explain why he did that, or maybe some other people who told you about the incident? Was there any particular reason why he went into that house and did that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Friends from my own village told me about it. They heard that Arkan had banned this in our area because he himself had started a business in Erdut, selling the final product, factory-made, not homemade. I didn't get any details, but that's what I understood from those friends who told me. But I neither dared, nor wanted to, nor intended to discuss it with him. Instead, I went to the highest possible place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain when you met with Milosevic and complained to him about it, what exactly did he mean when he mentioned those members of parliament?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that I understood him well. I understood what he meant. Perhaps I didn't quote him precisely, but now I will. He said, Arkan has five members of parliament, my parliament. I don't want him to cause problems to my party. He didn't want to confront him. That's what I understood. But I paraphrased it; it's not an exact quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further below in this document, General Panic mentions that several meetings were held to discuss this in 1992 and in 1993. He says Milosevic decided that such groups from Serbia be pulled out from Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina. We have looked only at one meeting, and perhaps there are documents from other meetings as well, but I'd like to know whether after 16 of April, 1992, or perhaps in 1993, anybody asked you to do something about Arkan and to have him withdrawn from the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me to do that because every normal person knew it would make absolutely no sense to ask me to do that. I was not capable of such a thing, and there was no reason to go to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn the page again in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The journalist asks him to go back to 1990-something and then it's not clear. He says: "Is it true that the volunteers had either to place themselves under your command or to leave the area? " The journalist says: "You said you ordered it."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now we need to move to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He says that they were given a choice to join the JNA or to leave. He said that they were formed at the initiative of some political groups. According to your knowledge, was this specific volunteer unit led by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, formed at the initiative of a political party or group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I knew, I can say with full responsibility that no one from the territory where I was formed them. So not in Slavonia, Baranja, or Western Srem, not from any political groups or any other groups. And apart from that, whatever I were to say, I would be speculating. I don't have any certain information about who formed them, even though there were rumours that Arkan was a colonel in the federal MUP, but that was just something I heard in the media and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move one page forward in the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The White Eagles and Seselj's Chetniks are also mentioned here. Please tell me, while you were the prime minister of SBWS did you have a chance to see these White Eagles, or Seselj's Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a chance to see them. From what I knew, they arrived in Slavonia and Baranja as parts of the JNA already. Whether that was the Serbian TO or the Yugoslav People's Army or, rather, the reservists from Serbia, but they were already uniformed and armed, that is to say uniformed, and then they were distributed arms by the JNA once they arrived. But that was what I learned indirectly. The same goes for the White Eagles. I didn't meet any of them, even though I heard that in my village, Pacetin, there were several of those volunteers but as part of the JNA under Mirko Jovic. They were his sympathisers. They were all the JNA. And they did not stay there long, just a couple of days. They were not undisciplined as it's claimed here. They were completely normal, and they didn't carry out any negative activities. That's what I heard from my neighbours later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Panic says here that he placed all the volunteer formations under his control and that it was only this group, the White Eagles, who had refused that but that then they expelled them. Do you know that by any chance?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't know under whose control they were, but I know under whose control they weren't. They were not under my control, nor did I have anything to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now move to a different topic, Mr. Hadzic. Could you tell us something about the contents -- the contacts you had with regard to exhumations at Ovcara and the talks you had about that. Can you briefly tell us how, according to your knowledge and recollection, you got involved in the talks that had to do with this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the talks reached my level, I then realised that I had heard how it all had developed, so I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission - I would call it an international one - those who requested that the possible mass grave be investigated, they contacted the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I was not involved in that, nor did I know about those contacts at the time. No one informed me. I later heard that there was not much opposition in Knin but that someone from the government proposed that this should be done reciprocally. And there may have been some logic to it. But from the humanitarian point of view, I wouldn't be in favour of that. The idea was that some mass graves where Serbs were should be investigated as well. That slowed down the negotiations and arrangements. Judging by the information I received later, some structures from the former JNA had attempted to impede that or slow it down. When the request reached me, I accepted, but I have explained and I have said that, as the president, I had nothing against it but that technically those next to me needed to give their approval - the government and everyone else - because I couldn't order them in anything. And I signed the agreement as soon as the request had reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D469. It is tab - sorry - 765.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is provided here is the timeline of events with regard to Ovcara. We can see here that the first talks on this issue were -- began in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me whether you knew at the time in March 1993 that the talks had begun. Did anyone address you at the time in connection with those talks?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one addressed me at the time, not yet, nor did I hear about this from my associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It follows from this that Prime Minister Bjegovic verbally confirmed the promises he had given earlier with regard to exhumations at Ovcara but that Mr. Milanovic opposed this. He set two conditions. As Mr. Milanovic was from SBWS, from the area, did you have any contacts with him about this? Did he tell you anything? Did he consult you about the position which he took at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milanovic was the assistant minister of defence, and I didn't have any special contacts with him. He didn't tell me anything about that at the time but I see that the date is the month of July when I was involved about the Erdut Agreement. I went to Geneva. I'm not sure about the exact dates, but I was often in Geneva during 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move one page forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that there was an opposition against -- again in October on part of Milan Milanovic who said that he wasn't aware that the exhumation had been approved by Knin. But before that, let's clarify just one issue. It says here that he was a colonel. Is it an error or did he really hold the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not have this rank at the time. But I heard that when he moved to Serbia after reintegration that he was given the rank of colonel. He was awarded that rank by the Serbian police. He had close contacts with Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move one page forward again. On the 20th of October, we can see again that the opposition by Sector East authorities was continued, particularly by Colonel Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this continued resistance coming from his part at this time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no one asked my assistance with regard to this at the time. Not yet. As soon I was involved, I gave my support to it. Minister Jarcevic informed me about this and asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move to page 5 of this document. Page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please just take into account that in September 1993 the Medak pocket operation was conducted and we were practically in a state of war, so all the talks and negotiations and everything else was postponed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the top of the page, we can read -- though the Medak [indiscernible] is discussed on the previous page. But on the following page, the 3rd of November, 1993, reads that the commission has decided to circulate a press release because it did not receive any feedback from Minister Bjegovic after his talks with you. And Mr. Bjegovic had previously said that he would talk with you because supposedly there was some opposition from the Supreme Defence Council. So what I'd like to know is this: This issue of exhumation at Ovcara, was it ever raised before the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in my presence. As far as I know, I think that it was not an issue that the Supreme Defence Council was supposed to discuss. I don't think it would come within military issues. For me, this was a humanitarian issue, and, of course, a criminal one, if the perpetrators were known.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, it says precisely that the government had given its authorisation for the exhumation at Ovcara: "However, the Supreme Defence Council of the RSK had a different view." That's the reason why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already replied, that it wasn't so. There were three members of the government on the Supreme Defence Council. They could have voted differently and made a different decision, outvoted the others, had they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bjegovic ask for your co-operation as indicated here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 3rd of November. The upper part of the text. Did he ask for your approval?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that he put it exactly in those words. He didn't ask for approval. When we had these talks, those were just consultations. He was not asking for my approval. But I don't think that between 30th October and 3rd November we would have been able to meet and discuss it. I think it could have been a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It follows from this that on the 11th of November, 1993, you addressed Mr. Fenrick for the first time. In fact, Mr. Jarcevic approached him saying that you would like to see him on 16 November in Erdut. And the text goes on -- on to the following page. Did you, indeed, let him know through Mr. Jarcevic that you wanted to see him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was after my consultations with Bjegovic, which would have been a day or two before. It was a delicate matter because it wasn't very well received by the Serbs who were saying, And where are our graves? Who's going to look after them? So it was a problem. And that's why, I suppose, Bjegovic wanted to consult me so that we can take a unified position, to avoid problems later. And I accepted it. I believed the humanitarian aspect is more important than anything else, and the most important thing is to see what actually happened there. I discussed similar issues with the ambassador of the European community, Mr. -- Mr. Ahrens. He said, Of course, it's not all right that people were killed but we have to find out what happened. There are wives of these men who still cannot get any benefits or exercise any rights before they get death certificates. I took it very seriously and, to the best of my ability, I worked for these matters to be settled. Of course, my ability was not great in this matter because most of these things had happened even before the Republic of Serbian Krajina was established and before I became its president.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Follows a description of that meeting held on 16 of November. We see that alongside you, there were Mr. Niksic, vice-chairman of the regional council, and Colonel Milanovic. It then lists your statements. Under (a), you say that the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina agree to co-operate and give their approval for the excavations on the site of Ovcara; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because Bjegovic told me that they agree, and then I was able to make this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say that the excavation activities would start in March or April when the weather improves and that you would appoint one member to observe the activities of the commission. And also that you approved all that is stated above and are willing to co-operate fully with the commission. Is all of this correct and faithfully reflected?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all correct, but I have to say at this point that, after that, there were elections where I lost, as everybody knows, and it all could not happen until I became the president of Slavonia, Baranja, after the Operation Storm. And I appointed a representative to attend the excavations that took place in 1996. So it didn't happen in the spring of 1994 as planned. But that proposal for spring 1994 came from Mr. Fenrick, who said that it simply couldn't be done in the current weather. He said, March or April next year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After this -- after this conversation on the 16 of November, 1993, and before 1996, as you explained now, were you ever contacted again on the issue of Ovcara and the excavation of victims?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. After I lost the elections, my status was very thankless. The police seized my car, and I was subjected to harassment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss this a bit later. You know that, among other things, you are charged under this indictment because the crimes against non-Serbs and other crimes in the Republic of Serbian Krajina were not adequately prosecuted and you allegedly did not do enough for perpetrators to be found and tried, so I'm going to ask you a few questions about that. First of all, when were courts established in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem after the beginning of hostilities and after the courts that existed until 25th June ceased to exist? When did the courts start working again?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although in 1991 there was military rule in the whole territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, our government started establishing courts towards the end of 1991, and I think they began to operate very soon afterwards; in the beginning of 1992, let's say. But I had no competencies in the area of the judiciary. As to your other point that one of the charges against me is that crimes were not prosecuted, that is not true. I have facts to prove it, and I will do so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any powers to order courts or other judiciary bodies to take a certain action or to make a certain decision? Were you able to tell them what to decide?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no such powers, and I didn't interfere with the work of the judiciary at all. Everybody knows how authority and power are divided in a democracy. There is the executive, the judicial, and the law-making branch. I was in the executive branch of authority, and I did not interfere with the work of the judiciary in any way, and I had nothing do with any prosecutions of any general crime or other crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able, did you have legal powers or practical ability to appoint whom you chose as prosecutors, presidents of courts, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. And I never tried to. We just left in those positions people who occupied them before the war. I didn't interfere in that sphere at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From what you know, were these judges professionally qualified for their job; namely, the qualifications stipulated by the earlier law for being appointment [as interpreted] to those positions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. They were qualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From what you personally know - and we're not going to go into any detail - did the judiciary function at all? The police, the prosecutor's office, and the courts, did they operate during the existence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem? Were perpetrators of crimes prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean 1991 or later?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us about both.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, it was military rule, and military security, military prosecutors, and military courts were in charge. That's at least how I understood it. Later on, there were courts, and they worked to the best of their ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if these courts and prosecutor's offices prosecuted the Serbs who had committed crimes against Croats and other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. In every case where perpetrators were identified, they were prosecuted. And investigations continued to be carried out even when perpetrators were not identified. In some case, we still can't know to this day who committed a particular murder. And I want to stress again: It was a thorn in the side for the policies that I was trying to carry through. Attacks against Croats, looting, robberies, murders. It was just undermining us politically. It went completely against all our political interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow, Mr. Zivanovic, how long will you take?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know how much time I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You have theoretically -- you have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will need maybe one to two hours more. I would -- I will do my best to finish by the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll try to do that. Mr. Hadzic, you're still a witness under oath. Court adjourned. We'll see each other at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of July, 2014, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
